sources.note: §3.4 Phonology (pp. 52-63: 3.4.1 Phonemes, 3.4.2 Syllable structure, 3.4.3 Processes) is the same material as the JIPA Illustration. Keywords carry stress marks (p. 53: 'Keywords are offered in phonemic transcription with syllable boundaries indicated by dots and stress by [ˈ]', e.g. ˈpa.nɘn 'hill', ka.ˈna.ɾan 'type of otter', ma.ˈna.pa.ɾa 'ring'), but there is no statement of where stress falls and no stress/prosody subsection anywhere in the table of contents.

sources.note: §3.3.3 Rasgos suprasegmentales (p. 30): 'Los rasgos suprasegmentales en la lengua chayahuita son: la duración, la aspiración, la glotalización y la nasalización', quoting Hart et al. 1976: 3 who treat these four as 'covocales'. Stress/acento is not listed or mentioned; the author explicitly defers a new phonological analysis ('no planeamos dar mayor detalle sobre este aspecto de la lengua').

sources.note: Language is not in the catalog and has no existing statements. Hart 1988 says nothing about where word stress falls; it only describes an emphatic accent (extra voice force + post-vocalic aspiration, written with an acute). Cannot be used as a placement statement. Compare Rojas-Berscia, Napurí & Wang 2020 (JIPA, held by the project in the same folder), which marks primary stress on the first or second syllable of every example word but gives no stress section either.
Nothing on stress; phonology tables sourced from Rojas-Berscia 2019 and Barraza 2005.

sources.note: No word-stress rule. p. 13 (Ortografía): 'Se emplea el acento ortográfico para indicar énfasis o intensidad' — the written accent marks emphasis, not lexical stress. p. 290 (Notas gramaticales §10.1.5 El vocativo y el énfasis): emphasis is produced 'con mayor fuerza de voz y agregando a la vocal acentuada un sonido parecido al de la j castellana', written with an acute on the 'sílaba acentuada'. The Guía de pronunciación (p. 14) discusses voicing 'después de la segunda sílaba', nasalisation and syncope but not stress.

sources.note: The only dedicated phonology of Shawi; every later description cites it. Its treatment of suprasegmentals ('covocales': length, aspiration, glottalisation, nasalisation) is the place a statement on accent/stress (or its absence) would be made. SIL has digitised the DEL series ( for DEL 7 at sil.org/resources/archives/30014), so a probably exists under an entry number that the bot-blocked search page hides.
